analysis.one_liner: Replaces the child tax credit and earned income tax credit with a guaranteed monthly payment for every child.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: introduced in April 2023 with 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until a subcommittee referral in December 2024, and died when the Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit and replace them with a monthly cash payment for every child under 19, set off the federal poverty guidelines. The payment would come from the Social Security Administration, with most children enrolled automatically unless their family opted out. It would also create two new $600 refundable credits: one for adults supporting dependents over 18, and one for adults aged 19 to 64, phasing out for incomes above $20,000 (or $40,000 for couples). It would be paid for with open-ended annual appropriations.
analysis.who_benefits: Families raising children, especially low- and moderate-income ones. Every child under 19 who resides in the U.S. and is a citizen, national, or qualified alien would get a monthly payment regardless of whether their parents work, and the payment would not count as income for other benefit programs like SNAP or housing assistance, so it would not push families off other aid. Adults supporting a dependent over 18 and childless adults aged 19 to 64 with modest incomes would also get new refundable credits.

how_it_helps.text: Every qualifying child under 19 would receive a monthly cash payment equal to one-twelfth of the gap between the federal poverty guideline for a two-person household and for a single person — roughly $400 per child per month at recent guideline levels.
Enrollment would be largely automatic: a child's social security number application or IRS records would be treated as an application for the payment unless the family affirmatively opts out.

The payment would be disregarded as both income and a resource when determining eligibility for any federal, state, or locally funded benefit program, so receiving it would not cost a family SNAP, housing, or other aid.

A new $600 refundable credit would cover each dependent over age 18, and a separate $600 credit ($1,200 for joint filers) would cover adults aged 19 to 64, phasing out at 5% of income above $20,000 for single filers and $40,000 for joint filers — a rare benefit for adults without children, whom the current tax code largely ignores.
The program would be run by a new Office of Universal Child Assistance inside the Social Security Administration, which already administers monthly benefits to tens of millions of Americans.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through annual appropriations with no offsetting revenue — the bill simply appropriates 'such sums as are necessary.' Families who currently receive more from the child tax credit or earned income tax credit than they would get under the new program would come out behind, and the repeal of the earned income tax credit removes a credit that currently rewards work.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers; some current credit recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the earned income tax credit outright, a credit that phases in with earnings and is generally understood to supplement the wages of working low-income parents; replacing it with a flat payment regardless of work removes that built-in work incentive.
It repeals the child tax credit for all families, including middle- and higher-income families who would not qualify for the new automatic payments at a level matching what they receive today.

The program is funded by an uncapped annual appropriation with no revenue source or pay-for, so its full multi-hundred-billion-dollar annual cost would simply be added to the deficit unless Congress separately raised revenue.

The bill directs the IRS to share taxpayer identity information — including citizenship, age, and residence of children — with the Social Security Administration to auto-enroll families, expanding the flow of tax data between agencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms the bill is a large, well-designed anti-poverty measure: automatic enrollment reaches families that fail to claim tax credits today, the income disregard prevents the payment from being clawed back through other programs, and the amount is pegged to the actual cost of raising a child at the poverty line. The serious tradeoffs are the loss of the earned income tax credit's work incentive, the repeal of a child tax credit that some middle-income families would not fully replace, and the absence of any funding source. Those tradeoffs were never tested in a hearing, because the bill never got one.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for its entire life; after twenty months with no hearing or markup, it was sent to a subcommittee in December 2024, where it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the End Child Poverty Act on April 6, 2023, joined by Reps. Jesús García of Illinois and Ilhan Omar as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
On December 17, 2024 — less than three weeks before the Congress ended — the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare, its only movement in twenty months.
The bill had 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and it never came to a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything new; the outcome preserved the status quo, leaving the existing child tax credit and earned income tax credit in place and no new child assistance program funded. The House Republican majority that controlled the Ways and Means Committee faced no political cost for taking no action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — no new program

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in twenty months; the committee took no action between the April 2023 referral and the December 2024 subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the committee calendar in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to languish without consideration until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the three original sponsors was joined by a Republican; the bill sat untouched in the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee for its entire life.

industries.industry: Paid tax preparation and refund-advance services
industries.note: The earned income tax credit repeal would remove one of the credits that most drives low-income families to paid preparers and refund-advance products. Automatic enrollment for the new child payment would further reduce the need to file a tax return to claim the benefit. This is a modest effect, and a simplification that benefits families.
